text.title: Graceful Offboard Script Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every agency-side client offboarding MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The offboard decision MUST cite at least two quantified bad-fit signals from the QBR source of record, each with its value and the target it misses: gross margin on the account below target for two or more consecutive quarters, scope-change requests outside contract above a stated count, days-to-pay above terms, team hours over budget by a stated percentage, or client satisfaction below a stated threshold. "Difficult client" or a single incident is not sufficient evidence.

rationale.source: Methodology design (QBR shows bad-fit client); account-management practice

rule.rationale: An offboard on gut feel is a decision the agency cannot defend to itself in six months, let alone to a client who asks why. Two data points from the QBR turn the exit from a mood into a pattern, and they are also what makes the internal record useful for changing intake criteria afterwards.

rule.statement: The script MUST frame the exit as a fit and alignment decision ("your needs have moved toward X; we are built for Y") and MUST NOT contain blame of the client, self-deprecation or a confession of failure. Banned phrases include "we could not deliver", "we failed", "we are not able to cope", "you have been difficult", "your team", followed by a criticism. Reviewers check the draft against the banned list and against the rule that every sentence about the client is neutral or positive.

rationale.source: Methodology design: strategic move, not a confession; reputation-management practice for professional services

rule.rationale: The words in the exit conversation are the words the client repeats to their network. A confession becomes "they admitted they could not handle it"; a blame becomes "they blamed us". A fit framing becomes "they were honest that we had outgrown each other and introduced us to someone", which is the only version that protects the referral pipeline.

rule.statement: The last service date MUST be no earlier than the contract's termination clause allows (notice period, minimum term, cure period), quoted by clause id in the artefact, and the script MUST state the last service date explicitly. Any prepaid or committed period MUST be delivered or refunded, and the artefact MUST say which. An exit date shorter than the clause, or a script with no date, is rejected.
rule.rationale: Ending early is a breach the client can invoice for, and it converts a graceful exit into a dispute in the same email. Stating the date and the clause removes ambiguity about who owes what and lets the client plan; a vague "over the coming weeks" leaves them guessing and resentful.

rule.statement: The script MUST be accompanied by a handover plan listing every asset the agency holds for the client (accounts and credentials, domains and DNS, ad and analytics accounts, source repositories, design files, content, documentation) with owner, transfer method and transfer date per asset, plus a transition-support window of stated length and cost (included or at a named rate). Assets the client owns MUST transfer regardless of any open commercial dispute; conditioning transfer on payment is permitted only where the contract grants it, quoted by clause id.

rationale.source: Agency-client contract practice on work-product ownership and termination assistance

rule.rationale: The handover is where reputations are actually won or lost. A client who receives their ad account, domain and repo on a schedule tells people the agency was professional to the end; a client who has to chase for a password tells people the agency held their assets hostage. The inventory makes the difference a checklist rather than a hope.

rule.statement: The script MUST name at least one specific alternative provider matched to the client's stated needs and offer a warm introduction. Before the alternative is named, the operator MUST have confirmed with that provider that they are willing to take the introduction, and the artefact MUST record the date and channel of that confirmation. Naming an unconfirmed provider, or a generic "there are many agencies who could help", is rejected.

rationale.source: Methodology design (handover plan plus recommended-alternative agency); referral-network practice

rule.rationale: The alternative is what turns an exit into a favour. A confirmed introduction gives the client a next step and the alternative agency a lead, which is how the offboard feeds the referral pipeline rather than draining it. An unconfirmed name that declines the client makes the agency look careless twice.

rule.statement: The offboard MUST be delivered first in a live conversation (call or meeting) by the named account owner, and the written script with the handover plan MUST follow within one business day. Email-only delivery is forbidden. The written follow-up MUST NOT contain anything that was not said in the conversation.

rationale.source: Professional-services relationship practice; methodology relationship-preservation goal

rule.rationale: An offboard by email is a breakup text: it is the detail the client remembers and repeats. The call lets the client react, ask about the handover and hear the fit framing in a human voice; the written follow-up makes it actionable. A written version that adds new points reads as the real message and the call as theatre.

rule.statement: A feedback or NPS request MUST be scheduled for 30 days after the last service date and recorded in the artefact. Where the response is a promoter score (9 or 10 on the 0 to 10 NPS scale) the operator MUST ask for a testimonial or a referral; where it is lower, the operator MUST reply with thanks and a single question about what would have changed the outcome, and MUST NOT argue. Silence after the last service date is forbidden.

rationale.source: Net Promoter Score (Reichheld, 2003, Harvard Business Review, The One Number You Need to Grow); methodology design (post-offboard NPS / testimonial request, not silence)

rule.rationale: Offboarded clients are the ones most likely to be asked "what happened with your agency?", and the answer depends on the last contact. A feedback request thirty days on says the agency still cares about the outcome; a promoter who was offboarded well is a credible referral precisely because they were not a customer any more.

rule.statement: The internal offboard record MUST assign the root cause to one primary category (pricing and margin, scope and expectations, capability fit, communication and working style, payment behaviour) and state the concrete change to the agency's intake or qualification criteria that follows from it. An offboard record that changes nothing in qualification MUST be flagged for review by the named consumer.

rationale.source: Methodology design (QBR-cycle retention review); continuous-improvement practice

rule.rationale: The same bad-fit client will be signed again next quarter unless the reason they were signed changes. The offboard is the most expensive piece of qualification data the agency ever collects; recording the root cause without changing the intake question is paying for the lesson and declining it.
